fields.name: BaseURL
fields.doc: BaseURL is the origin every relative path resolves against.

fields.name: DialTimeout
fields.doc: DialTimeout bounds establishing the TCP connection.

fields.name: HandshakeTimeout
fields.doc: HandshakeTimeout bounds the TLS handshake.

fields.name: ResponseTimeout
fields.doc:
ResponseTimeout bounds the wait for response headers after the request
has been written. It is separate from TotalTimeout so a slow upstream is
distinguishable from a large body.

fields.name: TotalTimeout
fields.doc: TotalTimeout bounds the whole call, body included.

fields.name: MaxResponseSize
fields.doc:
MaxResponseSize caps the response body in bytes. A body of exactly this
size is admitted; only one past it fails the call, and the body is never
truncated.

fields.name: MaxRedirects
fields.doc:
MaxRedirects caps the redirect chain. Every hop is re-authorised by the
policy, so a redirect cannot walk out of the allowed surface.

fields.name: DefaultHeaders
fields.doc: DefaultHeaders are added to every request that does not already set them.

symbols.doc:
ClientConfig describes an outbound client. Durations use DurationValue so a
configuration file can say "5s" rather than a nanosecond count.

It sits in core beside LimitsValue and TimeoutsValue, which carry the same
kind of knobs for the inbound half. Keeping both faces' configuration in one
layer is what lets a consumer decode a whole network stanza against the
contract package alone, without importing an implementation to name the type
of a field it is setting.

symbols.name: CodeAlreadyStarted
symbols.doc: CodeAlreadyStarted identifies a Start call on a server that is already serving.

symbols.name: CodeCallFailed
symbols.doc: CodeCallFailed identifies an outbound call that did not produce a response.

symbols.name: CodeConnLimitReached
symbols.doc:
CodeConnLimitReached identifies a connection rejected because the group's
concurrency ceiling was saturated.

symbols.name: CodeDrainTimeout
symbols.doc:
CodeDrainTimeout identifies a shutdown whose drain budget expired with
connections still in flight; the remainder is closed hard.

symbols.name: CodeGroupDuplicate
symbols.doc:
CodeGroupDuplicate identifies a second declaration of an already-declared
listener group name.

symbols.name: CodeGroupUnknown
symbols.doc: CodeGroupUnknown identifies a lookup for a listener group that was never declared.

symbols.name: CodeHandlerMissing
symbols.doc: CodeHandlerMissing identifies a listener group that was bound without a handler.

symbols.name: CodeHandlerPanic
symbols.doc:
CodeHandlerPanic identifies a panic recovered inside a handler; the connection
is closed but the process survives.

symbols.name: CodeInvalidAddress
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidAddress identifies a listen or dial address that is syntactically
unusable (empty host and port, malformed socket path, negative port).

symbols.name: CodeInvalidDuration
symbols.doc:
CodeInvalidDuration identifies a configuration duration that is neither a Go
duration literal nor an integer nanosecond count.

symbols.name: CodeListenFailed
symbols.doc: CodeListenFailed identifies a listener that could not be bound to its address.

symbols.name: CodeNotStarted
symbols.doc:
CodeNotStarted identifies an operation that requires a running server on one
that has not been started.

symbols.name: CodePacketTooLarge
symbols.doc: CodePacketTooLarge identifies a datagram longer than the group's accepted size.

symbols.name: CodeRequestDenied
symbols.doc:
CodeRequestDenied identifies an outbound request refused by the transport
policy before it left the process.

symbols.name: CodeResponseTooLarge
symbols.doc:
CodeResponseTooLarge identifies a response body that exceeded the configured
read ceiling.

symbols.name: CodeSSEFieldInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeSSEFieldInvalid identifies a Server-Sent Events frame the wire format
cannot carry: a line terminator inside an id, an event name or a comment
(the format has no escape — a newline SPLITS a value, so an id carrying one
would silently become a different id plus a stray field), a negative retry,
a retry under one millisecond (the wire field is an integer millisecond
count, and truncating to zero would say "reconnect immediately"), or a frame
with no field set at all.

symbols.name: CodeSSEFlushUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeSSEFlushUnsupported identifies a ResponseWriter that cannot be flushed.
Server-Sent Events is a streaming format: without a flush every event sits in
the transport buffer until the handler returns, which for an endless stream
means the client receives nothing, ever.

symbols.name: CodeSSEStreamClosed
symbols.doc:
CodeSSEStreamClosed identifies a send on a stream that has already ended —
the client disconnected, the server began draining, or the handler closed it.

symbols.name: CodeSSEStreamMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeSSEStreamMisconfigured identifies a stream option the domain refuses to
interpret rather than guess at: a negative keep-alive interval or a negative
per-write budget (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: CodeServerClosed
symbols.doc:
CodeServerClosed identifies work refused because the server already stopped
accepting; it is the expected terminal outcome of a graceful shutdown.

symbols.name: CodeSocketAdoptFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeSocketAdoptFailed identifies an inherited socket that could not be adopted
from the supervisor.

symbols.name: CodeStaticMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeStaticMisconfigured identifies a static file handler refused at
construction: no file tree to serve, a security header value the handler
will not send, or a Referrer-Policy token no browser recognises (ADR 0130).

symbols.name: CodeTLSHandshakeFailed
symbols.doc: CodeTLSHandshakeFailed identifies a TLS or mTLS handshake that did not complete.

symbols.name: CodeTLSMaterialInvalid
symbols.doc:
CodeTLSMaterialInvalid identifies TLS material that is absent, malformed, or
yields no usable certificate; it is never downgraded to an empty trust store.

symbols.name: CodeTooManyRedirects
symbols.doc: CodeTooManyRedirects identifies an outbound call that exceeded its redirect budget.

symbols.name: CodeUnsafePath
symbols.doc:
CodeUnsafePath identifies an outbound path carrying a dot segment, literal or
percent-encoded. Such a path is refused before any allowlist pattern is tried,
because an anchored pattern like ^/v1/supi/[^/]+$ happily matches "/v1/supi/.."
which the upstream then normalises to a different resource.

symbols.name: CodeUnsupportedNetwork
symbols.doc:
CodeUnsupportedNetwork identifies a network name the domain does not serve
(anything outside tcp, tcp4, tcp6, udp, udp4, udp6, unix, unixgram, unixpacket).

symbols.name: CodeWSConnClosed
symbols.doc:
CodeWSConnClosed identifies an operation on a connection that has ended — the
peer sent Close, the server began draining, the handler closed it, or the
socket died. It is the terminal outcome a receive loop runs until.

symbols.name: CodeWSConnMisconfigured
symbols.doc:
CodeWSConnMisconfigured identifies a connection option the domain refuses to
interpret rather than guess at: a negative ping interval or write budget, or
a non-positive size ceiling (ADR 0031).

symbols.name: CodeWSHandshakeFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeWSHandshakeFailed identifies an HTTP request that is not a valid RFC 6455
opening handshake: wrong method, absent or non-"websocket" Upgrade token, a
Connection header without "Upgrade", a Sec-WebSocket-Key that does not decode
to sixteen bytes, a Sec-WebSocket-Version other than 13, or an Origin the
server's policy refuses. The response is written before this is returned, so
the handler has nothing left to answer.

symbols.name: CodeWSInvalidPayload
symbols.doc:
CodeWSInvalidPayload identifies a payload the protocol cannot carry: a text
message or close reason that is not valid UTF-8 (§8.1), a close code that
must never appear on the wire (1004, 1005, 1006, 1015 and the unallocated
ranges — §7.4.2), or a close reason past the control-frame ceiling.

symbols.name: CodeWSMessageTooLarge
symbols.doc:
CodeWSMessageTooLarge identifies a frame or an accumulated message beyond the
connection's configured ceiling. The frame's announced length is checked
BEFORE any buffer is sized from it, because a 64-bit length field a peer
chooses is an out-of-memory condition one allocation away.

symbols.name: CodeWSProtocolViolation
symbols.doc:
CodeWSProtocolViolation identifies a frame RFC 6455 forbids: an unmasked
client frame (§5.1), a set reserved bit or reserved opcode (§5.2), a
fragmented or oversized control frame (§5.5), a non-minimal length encoding
(§5.2), a continuation with no message in progress or a new data frame
interrupting one (§5.4), or a malformed close payload (§5.5.1). Each fails
the connection.

symbols.name: CodeWSUpgradeUnsupported
symbols.doc:
CodeWSUpgradeUnsupported identifies a ResponseWriter whose connection cannot
be taken over — an HTTP/2 request, or a middleware wrapper that hides
http.Hijacker. WebSocket is not a response format: it replaces HTTP on the
socket, so without the hijack there is nothing to upgrade.

symbols.name: Conn
symbols.spelled: interface{Buffer() []byte; Group() string; ID() uint64; stdnet.Conn}
symbols.canonical: interface{Buffer() []byte; Group() string; ID() uint64; net.Conn}
symbols.doc:
Conn is one accepted stream connection.

It embeds stdlib net.Conn, so a handler reads and writes it exactly as it
would any socket and every io helper keeps working — io.Copy, bufio, encoding
wrappers, crypto/tls. Everything the domain adds is additive, which is what
keeps "plug a handler in" a four-line exercise.

A Conn is pooled and recycled once ServeConn returns. A handler MUST NOT
retain it, nor the slice returned by Buffer, past that point — the same
contract the logger's builder already carries.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete type stays unexported in internal/service/net/server.

symbols.name: Buffer
symbols.doc:
Buffer returns a connection-scoped scratch buffer sized by the group's
read-buffer limit. It is recycled with the connection, which is what lets
a handler read without allocating per connection.

symbols.name: Group
symbols.doc:
Group returns the name of the listener group that accepted this
connection, so one handler serving several groups can tell them apart.

symbols.name: ID
symbols.doc:
ID returns the monotonic identifier assigned at accept time, for
correlating log lines belonging to one connection.

symbols.name: ConnHandler
symbols.doc:
ConnHandler serves one accepted stream connection.

Returning an error does not kill the server: the connection is closed and the
error is logged and metered. That is deliberate — one malformed peer must
never be able to take down the process.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use: the server runs one
goroutine per connection and they all share the handler.

symbols.name: ConnHandlerFunc
symbols.doc: ConnHandlerFunc adapts a plain function to ConnHandler.

symbols.name: ServeConn
symbols.doc: ServeConn implements ConnHandler by calling f.

symbols.name: ConnLimitReached

code.public: The server is at its connection limit

symbols.doc: ConnLimitReached is returned when the group's connection ceiling is full.

symbols.name: DrainSignal
symbols.doc:
DrainSignal returns the drain channel carried by ctx, or nil when the server
serving this request publishes none.

A nil channel is the right absence: receiving from it blocks forever, so a
select that watches it alongside other cases simply never fires that case.
A caller therefore needs no nil check.

symbols.name: DrainTimeout

code.public: The server did not drain before its deadline

symbols.doc: DrainTimeout is returned when the shutdown drain budget expired.

symbols.name: DurationValue
symbols.doc:
DurationValue is a time.Duration that round-trips through JSON as either a Go
duration string ("30s", "1m30s") or a raw nanosecond count. The SDK's config
loader (ADR 0028) decodes through a JSON round-trip, and encoding/json renders
a bare time.Duration as nanoseconds — which would force an operator to write
30000000000 in a YAML file to mean thirty seconds. This type accepts both and
always emits the readable form.

The mixed receivers are required by encoding/json and are not a style slip:
MarshalJSON must take a value so a non-pointer struct field marshals, and
UnmarshalJSON must take a pointer so it can assign. The standard library's
time.Time carries the same asymmetry for the same reason.

PROMOTION CANDIDATE: this type is domain-neutral and stdlib-only, so it
belongs in internal/kernel or internal/core/app/config the moment a second domain
needs it. It is declared here because the repo's bar for a shared primitive is
two real consumers arising from an actual duplication, and today there is one.

symbols.name: Duration
symbols.doc: Duration returns the value as a plain time.Duration.

symbols.name: MarshalJSON
symbols.doc:
MarshalJSON emits the readable duration string so a written-back configuration
file stays legible.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String renders the canonical Go duration form, e.g. "1m30s".

symbols.name: UnmarshalJSON
symbols.doc:
UnmarshalJSON accepts a quoted Go duration string ("30s") or a bare number of
nanoseconds, so both a hand-written config file and a machine-generated one
decode.

symbols.name: GroupDuplicate

code.public: The listener group is already declared

symbols.doc: GroupDuplicate is returned for a second declaration of one group name.

symbols.name: GroupUnknown

code.public: The listener group is not declared

symbols.doc: GroupUnknown is returned for a lookup of an undeclared group.

symbols.name: HandlerMissing

code.public: The listener group has no handler

symbols.doc: HandlerMissing is returned when a group was bound without a handler.

symbols.name: HandlerPanic

code.public: The connection handler failed unexpectedly

symbols.doc: HandlerPanic wraps a panic recovered inside a handler.

fields.name: CertFile
fields.doc:
CertFile is the PEM leaf certificate followed by any intermediates.
Supplying it without KeyFile is always a configuration slip, never an
intention, and is refused: an mTLS client that silently degrades to plain
TLS is a security hole that reports nothing.

fields.name: KeyFile
fields.doc: KeyFile is the PEM private key matching CertFile.

fields.name: RootsFile
fields.doc:
RootsFile is the PEM CA bundle used to verify the peer. Leaving it empty
selects the platform trust store, which is right for a public endpoint and
wrong for a private PKI.

fields.name: ClientCAFile
fields.doc:
ClientCAFile is the PEM CA bundle a server accepts client certificates
from. Required whenever RequireClientCert is set.

fields.name: ServerName
fields.doc:
ServerName overrides the name verified against the peer certificate.

This is far more often required than its "optional" typing suggests. Any
deployment reached through a port forward or a tunnel connects to
127.0.0.1 while the peer certificate names the real service, and the
handshake then fails every single time until ServerName is set. Treat it
as mandatory whenever the dial address is not the certificate's name.

fields.name: MinVersion
fields.doc:
MinVersion is the lowest accepted TLS version. Zero selects TLS 1.3;
anything below TLS 1.2 is refused.

fields.name: NextProtos
fields.doc: NextProtos is the ALPN protocol list, e.g. {"h2", "http/1.1"}.

fields.name: RequireClientCert
fields.doc: RequireClientCert turns a server identity into mutual TLS.

symbols.doc:
IdentityFileParams names TLS material to read from the filesystem. Every path
is optional on its own; the combination is validated once the bytes are in
hand, by the same core constructor that validates in-memory material.

It is the disk-sourced twin of IdentityParams and lives beside it on purpose:
the two describe one domain concept — the material an identity is built from
— and splitting them across layers would let the rules that govern them drift
apart, which is exactly what this domain refuses for TLS.

symbols.name: IdentityParams
symbols.spelled: struct{CertPEM []byte; KeyPEM []byte; RootsPEM []byte; ClientCAPEM []byte; ServerName string; MinVersion uint16; NextProtos []string; RequireClientCert bool}
symbols.canonical: struct{CertPEM []byte; KeyPEM []byte; RootsPEM []byte; ClientCAPEM []byte; ServerName string; MinVersion uint16; NextProtos []string; RequireClientCert bool}

fields.name: CertPEM
fields.doc:
CertPEM is the PEM-encoded leaf certificate followed by any intermediates.
Paired with KeyPEM; supplying one without the other is an error.

fields.name: KeyPEM
fields.doc: KeyPEM is the PEM-encoded private key matching CertPEM.

fields.name: RootsPEM
fields.doc:
RootsPEM is the PEM-encoded CA bundle used to verify the peer. When empty
the platform trust store is used, which is the right default for a public
endpoint and the wrong one for a private PKI.

fields.name: ClientCAPEM
fields.doc:
ClientCAPEM is the PEM-encoded CA bundle a server accepts client
certificates from. It is meaningless on a client identity.

fields.name: ServerName
fields.doc:
ServerName overrides the name verified against the peer certificate. It is
required when connecting to a host by IP whose certificate names a DNS name.

fields.name: MinVersion
fields.doc:
MinVersion is the lowest accepted TLS version. Zero selects TLS 1.3;
anything below TLS 1.2 is refused outright.

fields.name: NextProtos
fields.doc: NextProtos is the ALPN protocol list, e.g. {"h2", "http/1.1"}.

fields.name: RequireClientCert
fields.doc:
RequireClientCert turns a server identity into mutual TLS: the peer must
present a certificate that chains to ClientCAPEM.

symbols.doc:
IdentityParams carries in-memory TLS material. Every field is optional on its
own; the combination is what is validated by NewIdentity. Sourcing material
from memory rather than from disk is what lets a consumer pull certificates
out of a secret manager without ever writing them to a filesystem.

symbols.name: IdentityValue
symbols.doc:
IdentityValue is an opaque TLS identity: a certificate chain, the trust
anchors used to verify the peer, and the negotiated-version policy. Its String
and GoString output is always "<redacted>" so an accidental %v, %s or %#v can
never spill key material into a log line. The only way out is ClientConfig or
ServerConfig, which mint a fresh *tls.Config per call.

The zero value is valid and means "no identity" — IsZero reports it.

symbols.name: ClientConfig
symbols.doc:
ClientConfig returns a fresh *tls.Config for dialling a peer. Each call yields
a new value so a caller mutating the result cannot affect any other user of
the same identity.

"Fresh" covers the slices and the trust pool, not only the outer struct. A
new *tls.Config whose Certificates and RootCAs still point at the identity's
own would leave cfg.Certificates[0] = other and cfg.RootCAs.AddCert(evil)
reaching every other configuration the identity has ever minted, including
ones already in use — which is the opposite of what an opaque, immutable
identity is for. Who pays that cost, and how often, is the CALLER's choice
and not a property of this method: net/client calls it once inside New and
net/server once per listener, but service/app/mail calls it per connection —
which for SMTP is per message — deliberately, because StartTLS takes the
config and a transport that reused one would hand every send a *tls.Config
another send could still be mutating. Three slice clones are nothing beside
an SMTP round trip; the sentence that used to sit here said "never per
request", which was true of the two net callers and false of the third.

symbols.name: GoString
symbols.doc:
GoString implements fmt.GoStringer so %#v stays redacted too — fmt bypasses
String for Go-syntax formatting and would otherwise dump the unexported fields.

symbols.name: IsZero
symbols.doc:
IsZero reports whether the identity carries no material at all, which is the
zero value a caller gets when no TLS was configured.

symbols.name: ServerConfig
symbols.doc:
ServerConfig returns a fresh *tls.Config for accepting connections, switching
to mutual TLS when the identity requires a client certificate.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc:
String implements fmt.Stringer and always redacts so key material never
reaches a log line through %v or %s.

symbols.name: InvalidAddress

code.public: The network address is not valid

symbols.doc: InvalidAddress is returned for a syntactically unusable address.

symbols.name: InvalidDuration

code.public: The duration value is not valid

symbols.doc:
InvalidDuration is returned for a configuration duration that parses as
neither a Go duration literal nor an integer nanosecond count.

symbols.name: LimitsValue
symbols.spelled: struct{MaxConns int "json:\"max_conns\""; ReadBufferSize int "json:\"read_buffer_size\""; MaxPacketSize int "json:\"max_packet_size\""; Backlog int "json:\"backlog\""; Shards int "json:\"shards\""; BatchSize int "json:\"batch_size\""}
symbols.canonical: struct{MaxConns int "json:\"max_conns\""; ReadBufferSize int "json:\"read_buffer_size\""; MaxPacketSize int "json:\"max_packet_size\""; Backlog int "json:\"backlog\""; Shards int "json:\"shards\""; BatchSize int "json:\"batch_size\""}

fields.name: MaxConns
fields.doc:
MaxConns caps concurrent connections in the group. Beyond it, a new
connection is accepted and immediately closed with ConnLimitReached, which
is kinder than letting the accept queue silently overflow.

fields.name: ReadBufferSize
fields.doc:
ReadBufferSize sizes the per-connection scratch buffer returned by
Conn.Buffer.

fields.name: MaxPacketSize
fields.doc:
MaxPacketSize is the largest datagram accepted. A larger one is DROPPED
and counted in StateValue.OversizedPackets, never delivered truncated:
the kernel discards the tail, so the prefix that survives reads exactly
like a complete message and the handler cannot tell the difference.

fields.name: Backlog
fields.doc: Backlog is the listen backlog depth where the platform honours it.

fields.name: Shards
fields.doc:
Shards is the number of independent listeners to open on one address with
SO_REUSEPORT, each with its own accept loop, to remove accept contention.
Zero selects the platform default.

fields.name: BatchSize
fields.doc:
BatchSize is how many datagrams to read per syscall. Zero selects the
default; one disables batching.

symbols.doc:
LimitsValue bounds what one listener group may consume. Every field is
optional; zero means "use the domain default", never "unbounded" — an unset
ceiling must not be the dangerous one.

symbols.name: ListenFailed

code.public: The server could not bind its listening address

symbols.doc: ListenFailed is returned when a listener could not be bound.

symbols.name: ListenerStateValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Group string "json:\"group\""; Address string "json:\"address\""; Network string "json:\"network\""; Shards int "json:\"shards\""; Degraded bool "json:\"degraded\""; DegradedReason string "json:\"degraded_reason,omitempty\""; Adopted bool "json:\"adopted\""}
symbols.canonical: struct{Group string "json:\"group\""; Address string "json:\"address\""; Network string "json:\"network\""; Shards int "json:\"shards\""; Degraded bool "json:\"degraded\""; DegradedReason string "json:\"degraded_reason,omitempty\""; Adopted bool "json:\"adopted\""}

fields.name: Group
fields.doc: Group is the listener group's name.

fields.name: Address
fields.doc:
Address is the address actually bound, which for a port of zero is the
one the kernel chose rather than the one requested.

fields.name: Network
fields.doc: Network is the socket family.

fields.name: Shards
fields.doc: Shards is how many listeners were actually opened on this address.

fields.name: Degraded
fields.doc:
Degraded reports that a requested optimisation was unavailable and the
server fell back. It is surfaced rather than logged once at startup,
because a silent fallback is indistinguishable from a working one and
nobody re-reads yesterday's logs to find out.

fields.name: DegradedReason
fields.doc: DegradedReason names the fallback in plain words when Degraded is set.

fields.name: Adopted
fields.doc:
Adopted reports a listener inherited from a supervisor rather than bound
by this process.

symbols.doc:
ListenerStateValue reports one bound listener.

It carries the address actually bound rather than the one requested, and it
reports any fallback explicitly, so a caller never has to infer either.

symbols.name: Middleware
symbols.doc:
Middleware decorates a handler with another of the same type.

It is generic over the handler type so stream and datagram handlers share one
shape and one Chain helper, instead of the domain carrying two near-identical
middleware types that would inevitably drift.

symbols.name: NewIdentityValue
symbols.doc:
NewIdentityValue validates in-memory TLS material and returns the opaque identity.
It fails loudly where the standard library is silent: a CA bundle that yields
no usable certificate is TLSMaterialInvalid, never an empty pool that would
verify nothing.

symbols.name: NotStarted

code.public: The server is not started

symbols.doc: NotStarted is returned when an operation requires a running server.

symbols.name: Packet
symbols.spelled: interface{Data() []byte; From() stdnet.Addr; Group() string; ID() uint64; Reply(b []byte) (n int, err error); To() stdnet.Addr}
symbols.canonical: interface{Data() []byte; From() net.Addr; Group() string; ID() uint64; Reply(b []byte) (n int, err error); To() net.Addr}
symbols.doc:
Packet is one received datagram.

Data is valid only until ServePacket returns: the buffer is recycled straight
back into the read batch, which is what makes batched datagram reading
allocation-free. A handler that needs the payload afterwards must copy it.

IFACE-PLUGIN: the concrete type stays unexported in internal/service/net/server.

symbols.name: Data
symbols.doc: Data returns the datagram payload.

symbols.name: From
symbols.doc: From returns the sender's address.

symbols.name: Group
symbols.doc: Group returns the name of the listener group that received it.

symbols.name: ID
symbols.doc: ID returns the monotonic identifier assigned at read time.

symbols.name: Reply
symbols.doc:
Reply writes a datagram back to the sender. It exists so the common case
needs no reference to the underlying connection.

symbols.name: To
symbols.doc: To returns the local address the datagram arrived on.

symbols.name: PacketHandler
symbols.doc:
PacketHandler serves one received datagram.

Returning an error does not kill the server: it is logged and metered, and
reading continues. A datagram service must survive a malformed packet.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use.

symbols.name: PacketHandlerFunc
symbols.doc: PacketHandlerFunc adapts a plain function to PacketHandler.

symbols.name: ServePacket
symbols.doc: ServePacket implements PacketHandler by calling f.

symbols.name: PacketTooLarge

code.public: The datagram is larger than the accepted size

symbols.doc:
PacketTooLarge names the reason a datagram beyond the group's accepted
size is dropped. It is deliberately not returned to anyone: a read loop
has no caller, so the drop is reported through
StateValue.OversizedPackets. The sentinel stays because it is what gives
that count a documented name in the registry.

symbols.name: Phase
symbols.doc:
Phase is where a server sits in its lifecycle. It is reported by State so an
operator — or a readiness probe — can tell "not yet listening" apart from
"listening" and from "draining", which a single boolean cannot express.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String renders the phase for logs and status output.

symbols.name: PhaseDraining
symbols.doc: PhaseDraining has stopped accepting and is waiting for in-flight work.

symbols.name: PhaseNew
symbols.doc: PhaseNew is a constructed server that has not bound anything yet.

symbols.name: PhaseServing
symbols.doc: PhaseServing is bound and accepting.

symbols.name: PhaseStarting
symbols.doc: PhaseStarting is binding listeners; some may already be up.

symbols.name: PhaseStopped
symbols.doc: PhaseStopped has released every listener.

symbols.name: Policy
symbols.doc:
Policy authorises an outbound request before it leaves the process.

The contract that makes this worth a port: implementations are evaluated
inside the RoundTripper, underneath every call site. A caller cannot construct
a request that skips the check, so "this client is read-only" becomes a
property of the code rather than a convention the next contributor must
remember. Allow returns nil to permit the request and a typed error to refuse
it; the refusal is reported as RequestDenied without echoing the path, so a
denial cannot leak the private API surface through a log line.

Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use.

IFACE-PLUGIN: concrete policies live in internal/service/net/client; their
types stay unexported behind their constructors.

symbols.name: PolicyFunc
symbols.doc: PolicyFunc adapts a plain function to the Policy interface.

symbols.name: Allow
symbols.doc: Allow implements Policy by calling f.

symbols.name: RequestDenied

code.public: The request was refused by policy

symbols.doc:
RequestDenied is returned when the transport policy refused an outbound call.
The public message never names the refused path, so a denial cannot leak the
shape of the private API surface through a log line.

symbols.name: RequestValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Method string; Scheme string; Host string; EscapedPath string; RawQuery string}
symbols.canonical: struct{Method string; Scheme string; Host string; EscapedPath string; RawQuery string}

fields.name: Method
fields.doc: Method is the uppercase HTTP method, e.g. "GET".

fields.name: Scheme
fields.doc: Scheme is the URL scheme, e.g. "https".

fields.name: Host
fields.doc:
Host is the authority, host[:port]. It is carried because a policy that
sees only the path cannot defend against a redirect that keeps the path
and swaps the origin.

fields.name: EscapedPath
fields.doc:
EscapedPath is the percent-encoded path exactly as it will be sent. It is
never the decoded form — see the type comment.

fields.name: RawQuery
fields.doc: RawQuery is the encoded query string, without the leading "?".

symbols.doc:
RequestValue describes an outbound request to the transport policy.

Two field choices are load-bearing and were paid for in a real integration:

  - The path is the ESCAPED form, the one that goes on the wire. url.URL.Path
    is already percent-DECODED, so a policy that judges it accepts "%2e%2e"
    — which the upstream then reinterprets as "..". Judging the decoded form
    makes a correctly written allowlist bypassable, so this type does not
    carry it.
  - RawQuery is present because a policy often needs to require a parameter,
    not just permit a path. A read-only policy that cannot see the query
    cannot, for instance, insist that a listing call passes the filter that
    makes its result correct.

The value is immutable by construction: a policy receives a copy and cannot
mutate the request it is judging.

symbols.name: ResponseTooLarge

code.public: The response is larger than the accepted size

symbols.doc: ResponseTooLarge is returned when a response body exceeded the read ceiling.

symbols.name: ResponseValue

fields.name: Status
fields.doc:
Status is the HTTP status code. It is set even when the call also returns
an error, so a caller can tolerate a specific status deliberately.

fields.name: Header
fields.doc: Header is the response header set.

fields.name: Body
fields.doc:
Body is the fully-read response body, already bounded by the client's
size cap. It is nil for a status that carries no body, such as 204.

symbols.doc:
ResponseValue is a fully-read outbound response.

The client returns this rather than an *http.Response on purpose. A returned
*http.Response makes the caller responsible for closing the body and for
reading it under a size cap, and a single forgotten Close leaks a connection.
It also makes an accurate byte count impossible: the size of a body is only
known once it has been read, so an observation hook firing at header time can
never report it. Reading and closing inside the client fixes both.

symbols.name: SSEContentType
symbols.doc:
SSEContentType is the media type an event stream must be served under. A
client that receives anything else does not start an EventSource at all.

symbols.name: SSEEventValue
symbols.spelled: struct{ID string "json:\"id\""; Name string "json:\"event\""; Data string "json:\"data\""; Retry DurationValue "json:\"retry\""}
symbols.canonical: struct{ID string "json:\"id\""; Name string "json:\"event\""; Data string "json:\"data\""; Retry github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.DurationValue "json:\"retry\""}

fields.name: ID
fields.doc:
ID is the frame's "id" field. A client stores the last non-empty id it
saw and sends it back as Last-Event-ID when it reconnects, so this is the
resume token — and it is the CALLER's to mint, because only the caller
knows what it means. Empty emits no id field, which leaves the client's
stored id untouched; that is the format's own behaviour, not an omission.

fields.name: Name
fields.doc:
Name is the frame's "event" field — the event type the client dispatches
under. Empty means the default type, "message".

fields.name: Data
fields.doc:
Data is the payload. Every line terminator it carries (LF, CR or CRLF)
becomes a separate "data:" line, which the client rejoins with "\n". A
payload that mixed terminators therefore arrives normalised to LF: the
value is preserved, its byte spelling is not.

fields.name: Retry
fields.doc:
Retry is the reconnection delay hint, emitted as an integer millisecond
count. Zero emits no retry field.

symbols.doc:
SSEEventValue is one Server-Sent Events frame.

The format has no escape mechanism. A line terminator inside a value is not
quoted, it SPLITS the value: that is exactly what makes a multi-line payload
expressible — Data is emitted as one "data:" line per line and the client
rejoins them with "\n" — and exactly what makes a line terminator inside ID
or Name unrepresentable. Those are refused rather than truncated, because a
silently shortened id is a resume token pointing at the wrong place.

symbols.name: IsZero
symbols.doc: IsZero reports whether the frame carries no field at all.

symbols.name: Validate
symbols.doc:
Validate reports whether the frame can be carried by the wire format.

It is separate from the encoder (internal/service/net/sse.AppendEvent) so a
caller can check a frame before committing to send it, and so the encoder
can validate everything BEFORE it appends anything — a half-written frame on
a stream is unrecoverable, since the peer has already read it.

symbols.name: SSEFieldInvalid

code.public: The event cannot be represented in the event-stream format

symbols.doc:
SSEFieldInvalid is returned for a Server-Sent Events frame the wire format
cannot carry. The format has no escape mechanism: a newline inside a value
SPLITS it rather than being quoted, so an id or an event name carrying one
would arrive as a different value plus a stray field. It is refused, never
truncated — a silently shortened id is a resume token that points at the
wrong place.

symbols.name: SSEFlushUnsupported

code.public: The response cannot be streamed

symbols.doc:
SSEFlushUnsupported is returned when the ResponseWriter cannot be flushed.
Without a flush the events accumulate in the transport buffer and reach the
client only when the handler returns, so an endless stream delivers nothing
at all — the failure is total and silent, which is why it is refused at
construction rather than discovered in production.

symbols.name: SSELastEventIDHeader
symbols.doc:
SSELastEventIDHeader is the request header a reconnecting client sends,
carrying the id of the last event it processed.

symbols.name: SSEMinRetry
symbols.doc:
SSEMinRetry is the smallest reconnection hint the wire can carry. The retry
field is an integer MILLISECOND count, so anything shorter rounds to zero —
and zero does not mean "a very short delay", it means "reconnect at once".

symbols.name: SSEStreamClosed

code.public: The event stream is closed

symbols.doc:
SSEStreamClosed is returned by a send on a stream that has already ended:
the client disconnected, the server began draining, or the handler closed
it. It is the terminal outcome a streaming handler loops until.

symbols.name: SSEStreamMisconfigured

code.public: The event stream options are not valid

symbols.doc:
SSEStreamMisconfigured is returned for a stream option the domain refuses
to interpret rather than guess at (ADR 0031). A zero keep-alive interval is
CLAMPED to the domain default, because a working keep-alive needs no
explanation; a negative one is REFUSED, because no value the SDK invented
for it would be defensible and "never" already has an explicit spelling.

symbols.name: ServerClosed

code.public: The server is closed

symbols.doc: ServerClosed is returned once the server has stopped accepting work.

symbols.name: SocketAdoptFailed

code.public: An inherited socket could not be adopted

symbols.doc: SocketAdoptFailed is returned when an inherited socket could not be adopted.

symbols.name: StateValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Phase Phase "json:\"phase\""; Listeners []ListenerStateValue "json:\"listeners\""; ActiveConns int64 "json:\"active_conns\""; TotalConns uint64 "json:\"total_conns\""; RejectedConns uint64 "json:\"rejected_conns\""; OversizedPackets uint64 "json:\"oversized_packets\""; AcceptBackoffs uint64 "json:\"accept_backoffs\""}
symbols.canonical: struct{Phase github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.Phase "json:\"phase\""; Listeners []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/net.ListenerStateValue "json:\"listeners\""; ActiveConns int64 "json:\"active_conns\""; TotalConns uint64 "json:\"total_conns\""; RejectedConns uint64 "json:\"rejected_conns\""; OversizedPackets uint64 "json:\"oversized_packets\""; AcceptBackoffs uint64 "json:\"accept_backoffs\""}

fields.name: Phase
fields.doc: Phase is where the server sits in its lifecycle.

fields.name: Listeners
fields.doc: Listeners describes every bound listener, including any degradation.

fields.name: ActiveConns
fields.doc: ActiveConns is the number of connections currently being served.

fields.name: TotalConns
fields.doc: TotalConns is the number accepted since the server started.

fields.name: RejectedConns
fields.doc: RejectedConns is the number turned away by the connection ceiling.

fields.name: OversizedPackets
fields.doc:
OversizedPackets is the number of datagrams dropped for passing their
group's MaxPacketSize. They are counted rather than delivered because the
kernel has already discarded the tail, and the prefix that survives is
indistinguishable from a complete message to the handler receiving it. A
read loop has nobody to return an error to, so this counter is the report.

fields.name: AcceptBackoffs
fields.doc:
AcceptBackoffs is the number of times an accept loop waited after Accept
failed with anything but its listener closing — the process out of file
descriptors, typically, with connections still queued. Retrying at once
would spin a core per listener while the condition lasts; each wait is
5 ms, doubling to 1 s, and the next accepted connection starts the curve
over. A count that keeps rising is a server that cannot accept.

symbols.doc:
StateValue is a snapshot of the server's lifecycle and listeners.

It is a value, so a caller can hold it, log it, or compare it without racing
the server that produced it.

symbols.name: Degraded
symbols.doc:
Degraded reports whether any listener fell back from a requested
optimisation, so a caller can assert "no silent degradation" in one call
instead of walking the slice.

symbols.name: StaticMisconfigured

code.public: The static file handler configuration is not valid

symbols.doc:
StaticMisconfigured is returned when a static file handler is built with
nothing it can serve safely: no file tree, a header value carrying a
control character, or a Referrer-Policy token no browser knows — which a
browser ignores, silently falling back to a weaker default. The "option"
field names which (ADR 0130).

symbols.name: TLSHandshakeFailed

code.public: The TLS handshake failed

symbols.doc: TLSHandshakeFailed is returned when a TLS or mTLS handshake did not complete.

symbols.name: TLSMaterialInvalid

code.public: The TLS material is missing or invalid

symbols.doc:
TLSMaterialInvalid is returned for absent, malformed, or empty TLS material.
It is deliberately loud: an unusable bundle must never degrade into a trust
store that silently verifies nothing.

symbols.name: TimeoutsValue
symbols.spelled: struct{Read DurationValue "json:\"read\""; Write DurationValue "json:\"write\""; Idle DurationValue "json:\"idle\""; Handshake DurationValue "json:\"handshake\""}

fields.name: Read
fields.doc: Read bounds one read from the peer.

fields.name: Write
fields.doc: Write bounds one write to the peer.

fields.name: Idle
fields.doc: Idle bounds how long a connection may sit with no traffic at all.

fields.name: Handshake
fields.doc:
Handshake bounds the TLS handshake, which is the phase a hostile peer can
most cheaply stall. Unlike the others, zero here does NOT mean unbounded:
the negotiation happens before any handler exists to notice it, so it
falls back to the domain's default instead.

symbols.doc:
TimeoutsValue bounds each phase of a connection separately.

Per-phase deadlines rather than one overall budget: a slow reader, a slow
writer and an idle keep-alive connection are three different problems with
three different right answers, and a single timeout cannot tell them apart.

Every field is a PER-OPERATION bound, refreshed each time, not a budget for
the connection's whole life. The distinction is the whole point: a peer
sending one byte per second violates a per-read bound at once and stays
inside a lifetime bound until the lifetime runs out.

symbols.name: TooManyRedirects

code.public: The outbound call exceeded its redirect budget

symbols.doc: TooManyRedirects is returned when a call exceeded its redirect budget.

symbols.name: UnsafePath

code.public: The request path is not in normalised form

symbols.doc:
UnsafePath is returned for a path carrying a dot segment in any form. It is
evaluated before the allowlist, because Go normalises dot segments neither
in url.URL nor in the transport, so an anchored pattern alone is not enough.

symbols.name: UnsupportedNetwork

code.public: The network type is not supported

symbols.doc: UnsupportedNetwork is returned for a network name outside the served set.

symbols.name: WSAcceptHeader
symbols.doc: WSAcceptHeader carries the server's proof it understood the handshake.

symbols.name: WSBinary
symbols.doc: WSBinary carries opaque bytes.

symbols.name: WSClose
symbols.doc: WSClose begins or completes the closing handshake.

symbols.name: WSCloseAbnormal
symbols.doc:
WSCloseAbnormal means the connection died without a Close frame. It is
reported to the application and never sent.

symbols.name: WSCloseCode
symbols.doc: WSCloseCode is the status code a Close frame carries (RFC 6455 §7.4).

symbols.name: Echoable
symbols.doc:
Echoable returns the code to send back when answering this one.

It exists because §5.5.1 says an endpoint SHOULD echo the peer's status code,
and the one code a peer can leave us holding — WSCloseNoStatus, for a Close
with no payload — is a code §7.4.1 forbids on the wire. Echoing blindly is
therefore a protocol error waiting for the first well-behaved peer that
closes without saying why.

symbols.name: Sendable
symbols.doc:
Sendable reports whether the code may appear in a Close frame on the wire.

It is deliberately a property of the CODE rather than a check inside the
sender, because the same question is asked twice from opposite directions: a
peer that sends 1006 is committing a protocol error, and so is this endpoint
if it ever does. One predicate, both directions, no chance of the two
drifting apart.

symbols.name: WSCloseExtensionRequired
symbols.doc:
WSCloseExtensionRequired is a client giving up because the server did not
negotiate an extension it needs. A server never sends it.

symbols.name: WSCloseGoingAway
symbols.doc:
WSCloseGoingAway is a server shutting down or a browser navigating away.
It is what a drain sends.

symbols.name: WSCloseInternalError
symbols.doc: WSCloseInternalError is an unexpected condition on this side.

symbols.name: WSCloseInvalidPayload
symbols.doc:
WSCloseInvalidPayload is a text frame that is not valid UTF-8, or a close
reason that is not.

symbols.name: WSCloseNoStatus
symbols.doc:
WSCloseNoStatus means the peer's Close frame carried no code. It is
reported to the application and never sent.

symbols.name: WSCloseNormal
symbols.doc: WSCloseNormal is a completed purpose, on either side.

symbols.name: WSClosePolicyViolation
symbols.doc: WSClosePolicyViolation is the generic refusal when no other code fits.

symbols.name: WSCloseProtocolError
symbols.doc: WSCloseProtocolError is a frame the RFC forbids.

symbols.name: WSCloseTLSHandshake
symbols.doc:
WSCloseTLSHandshake means the TLS handshake failed. It is reported to the
application and never sent — there is no connection to send it on.

symbols.name: WSCloseTooLarge
symbols.doc: WSCloseTooLarge is a message beyond what this endpoint accepts.

symbols.name: WSCloseUnsupportedData
symbols.doc:
WSCloseUnsupportedData is a well-formed frame carrying data this endpoint
cannot accept — binary to a text-only peer, for instance.

symbols.name: WSConnClosed

code.public: The WebSocket connection is closed

symbols.doc:
WSConnClosed is returned by any operation on a connection that has ended.
It is the terminal outcome a receive loop runs until, and it carries the
close code the peer sent when there was one.

symbols.name: WSConnMisconfigured

code.public: The WebSocket options are not valid

symbols.doc:
WSConnMisconfigured is returned for an option the domain refuses to
interpret rather than guess at (ADR 0031). A zero ping interval is CLAMPED
to the domain default, because a working heartbeat needs no explanation; a
negative one is REFUSED, and "never" has its own spelling.

symbols.name: WSContinuation
symbols.doc: WSContinuation continues the message the previous frame began.

symbols.name: WSExtensionsHeader
symbols.doc:
WSExtensionsHeader carries the extension offer. This domain negotiates
none, so it is never echoed — see the package CLAUDE.md.

symbols.name: WSGUID
symbols.doc:
WSGUID is the fixed string RFC 6455 §1.3 concatenates to Sec-WebSocket-Key
before hashing. It is a constant of the protocol, not a secret and not a
parameter: its only job is to make the accept value impossible to produce by
echoing the request, so a cache or a naive proxy cannot fake an upgrade.

symbols.name: WSHandshakeFailed

code.public: The WebSocket handshake is not valid

symbols.doc:
WSHandshakeFailed is returned when an HTTP request is not a valid RFC 6455
opening handshake. The upgrade is refused with an HTTP status rather than
a Close frame, because at that point there is no WebSocket connection to
close — the response is still an ordinary HTTP one.

symbols.name: WSInvalidPayload

code.public: The WebSocket payload is not valid

symbols.doc:
WSInvalidPayload is returned for a payload the protocol cannot carry: text
that is not UTF-8, a close code that must never be sent, or a close reason
past the control-frame ceiling. It is one sentinel for both directions on
purpose — the rule a peer broke is the rule this endpoint must not break.

symbols.name: WSKeyHeader
symbols.doc: WSKeyHeader carries the client's 16 random bytes, base64-encoded.

symbols.name: WSKeyLen
symbols.doc:
WSKeyLen is how many bytes Sec-WebSocket-Key decodes to (RFC 6455 §4.1).
A key of any other length is not a WebSocket handshake, whatever it decodes.

symbols.name: WSMaxControlPayload
symbols.doc:
WSMaxControlPayload is the ceiling RFC 6455 §5.5 puts on a control frame's
payload. It exists so an endpoint can answer a Ping without buffering: a
control frame is answered inline, between the fragments of a message, so it
must fit in a fixed buffer that is always available.

symbols.name: WSMessageTooLarge

code.public: The WebSocket message is larger than the accepted size

symbols.doc:
WSMessageTooLarge is returned when a frame or a reassembled message exceeds
the connection's ceiling. The check runs against the ANNOUNCED length,
before any buffer is sized from it: allocating from a 64-bit integer the
peer chose is a denial of service in one line.

symbols.name: WSMessageValue

fields.name: Binary
fields.doc:
Binary reports whether the payload is opaque bytes (opcode 0x2) rather
than UTF-8 text (opcode 0x1). The zero value is text, which is the
opcode a zero-valued frame would carry anyway.

fields.name: Data
fields.doc:
Data is the reassembled payload. For a text message it is valid UTF-8,
which the engine verifies on both the receiving and the sending side.

symbols.doc:
WSMessageValue is one complete WebSocket application message, reassembled
from however many frames carried it.

A message is the unit an application reasons about; a frame is the unit the
transport reasons about. Handing the application frames would make
fragmentation — which is the sender's private choice of chunk size, not a
semantic boundary — visible in every consumer.

symbols.name: OpCode
symbols.doc: OpCode returns the frame opcode this message is carried under.

symbols.name: WSOpCode
symbols.doc: WSOpCode is a frame's four-bit type field (RFC 6455 §5.2).

symbols.name: Defined
symbols.doc: Defined reports whether RFC 6455 assigns this opcode a meaning.

symbols.name: IsControl
symbols.doc:
IsControl reports whether the opcode names a control frame.

Control frames are the ones that may be injected BETWEEN the fragments of a
message, so the distinction decides which fragmentation rules apply.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String renders the opcode for a log line or an error field.

symbols.name: WSPing
symbols.doc: WSPing asks the peer to answer with a Pong carrying the same payload.

symbols.name: WSPong
symbols.doc: WSPong answers a Ping, or is sent unsolicited as a one-way heartbeat.

symbols.name: WSProtocolHeader
symbols.doc: WSProtocolHeader carries the subprotocol list, then the single choice.

symbols.name: WSProtocolViolation

code.public: The WebSocket frame is not valid

symbols.doc:
WSProtocolViolation is returned for a frame RFC 6455 forbids. Every case it
covers FAILS THE CONNECTION rather than being skipped: a peer that sent a
frame this endpoint ignored believes it said something, and the two would
be desynchronised from that point on.

symbols.name: WSText
symbols.doc: WSText carries a UTF-8 payload, validated on both sides.

symbols.name: WSUpgradeToken
symbols.doc: WSUpgradeToken is the token both Upgrade headers must carry.

symbols.name: WSUpgradeUnsupported

code.public: The connection cannot be upgraded

symbols.doc:
WSUpgradeUnsupported is returned when the response's connection cannot be
hijacked. It is deliberately distinct from a failed handshake: the request
was fine and the peer did nothing wrong — this stack cannot take over the
socket, which is a deployment fact (HTTP/2, or a middleware that wraps the
ResponseWriter without forwarding Unwrap), not a client error.

symbols.name: WSVersion
symbols.doc:
WSVersion is the only protocol version this domain speaks (RFC 6455 §4.1).
A request naming any other version is refused WITH this value advertised
back, which is what lets a client renegotiate instead of guessing.

symbols.name: WSVersionHeader
symbols.doc:
WSVersionHeader carries the client's version, and the server's
counter-offer when it refuses one.

symbols.name: WithDrainSignal
symbols.doc:
WithDrainSignal returns ctx carrying the channel a server closes when it
begins draining.

A request context is deliberately NOT what carries this. Cancelling it would
tell every in-flight handler to abandon the response it is halfway through,
which is the opposite of a graceful drain — the drain exists so those
responses finish. This signal is additive: a handler that ignores it behaves
exactly as before, and a handler that holds a connection open indefinitely —
an event stream, a long poll — gets the one piece of information it cannot
otherwise have, namely that finishing now is the cooperative thing to do.

The channel is closed, never sent on, so every observer sees it and a late
observer sees it immediately.

symbols.name: AnyValue
symbols.doc:
AnyValue builds a Value of KindAny carrying an arbitrary payload. Handlers
inspect the concrete type via type assertion and fall back to "?" when the
type is not in their format table.

symbols.name: AttrValue

fields.name: Key
fields.doc: Key identifies the attribute in the output line.

fields.name: Value
fields.doc: Value carries the typed payload; handlers dispatch on Value.Kind().

symbols.doc:
AttrValue is an immutable key/value pair carried by a RecordEvent. Use the
typed Value constructors (StringValue, Int64Value, …) to build the Value
field — the zero Value is a valid KindAny carrying nil.

symbols.name: BoolValue
symbols.doc: BoolValue builds a Value of kind bool.

symbols.name: CodeCtxCancelled
symbols.doc: CodeCtxCancelled identifies a Handle call whose context was already done.

symbols.name: CodeEncoderNil
symbols.doc: CodeEncoderNil identifies a NewHandler call made with a nil Encoder.

symbols.name: CodeHandlerNil
symbols.doc: CodeHandlerNil identifies a New call made with a nil core.Handler.

symbols.name: CodeSinkRequired
symbols.doc: CodeSinkRequired identifies a NewHandler call made with a nil Sink.

symbols.name: CodeWriteFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeWriteFailed identifies a Handle call whose underlying writer returned
a non-nil error; ExitCode defaults to 74 (EX_IOERR) for this case.

symbols.name: CodeWriterNil
symbols.doc: CodeWriterNil identifies a NewTextHandler call made with a nil io.Writer.

symbols.name: CtxCancelled

code.public: Logging aborted due to cancellation

symbols.doc: CtxCancelled wraps a cancelled context at Handle time.

symbols.name: DurationValue
symbols.doc:
DurationValue builds a Value of kind duration. Storing the int64 nanosecond
count in bits keeps the hot path allocation-free.

symbols.name: Encoder
symbols.spelled: interface{Append(dst []byte, groups []string, r RecordEvent) (out []byte); Name() (name string)}
symbols.doc:
Encoder formats a RecordEvent into a byte slice. Implementations MUST be
safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines and SHOULD avoid allocating
beyond the caller-supplied buffer (typically borrowed from the
kernel/concur/buffer pool) so the encoding step itself does not allocate.

symbols.name: Append
symbols.doc:
Append serialises r onto dst and returns the (possibly re-allocated)
buffer. groups carries the active group prefix stack — encoders are
responsible for rendering it as their format-specific prefix
("g1.g2.key" for text, nested objects for JSON).

symbols.name: Name
symbols.doc:
Name returns the canonical encoder identifier ("text", "ndjson",
"json"). Useful for diagnostic dumps and metrics tagging.

symbols.name: EncoderNil

code.public: Logger handler requires a non-nil encoder

symbols.doc: EncoderNil is returned when NewHandler receives a nil Encoder.

symbols.name: Float64Value
symbols.doc: Float64Value builds a Value of kind float64.

symbols.name: GroupValue
symbols.doc:
GroupValue builds a Value whose payload is a slice of AttrValue, modelling
a nested attribute group. The slice is stored verbatim — callers MUST NOT
mutate it after the Value is constructed.

symbols.name: Handler
symbols.spelled: interface{Enabled(ctx context.Context, r RecordEvent) (enabled bool); Handle(ctx context.Context, r RecordEvent) (err error); WithAttrs(attrs []AttrValue) (child Handler); WithGroup(name string) (child Handler)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Enabled(ctx context.Context, r github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.RecordEvent) (enabled bool); Handle(ctx context.Context, r github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.RecordEvent) (err error); WithAttrs(attrs []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.AttrValue) (child github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.Handler); WithGroup(name string) (child github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.Handler)}
symbols.doc:
Handler formats and emits RecordEvent values produced by a Logger.
Implementations MUST be safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines.

symbols.name: Enabled
symbols.doc:
Enabled reports whether the handler would emit a record at the given
level, allowing callers to skip expensive attribute construction.

symbols.name: Handle
symbols.doc:
Handle formats and writes a RecordEvent. Returning a non-nil error
signals a sink failure; the Logger may drop the record regardless.

symbols.name: WithAttrs
symbols.doc:
WithAttrs returns a derived Handler that prepends the given attrs to
every subsequent RecordEvent. The receiver MUST NOT be mutated.

symbols.name: WithGroup
symbols.doc:
WithGroup returns a derived Handler that namespaces every subsequent
attribute key under the given group name (rendered as "group.key"
for text handlers, or as a nested object for structured handlers).
An empty name MUST be treated as a no-op so callers can pass user
input without guarding it.

symbols.name: HandlerNil

code.public: Logger requires a non-nil handler

symbols.doc: HandlerNil is returned when New receives a nil Handler.

symbols.name: Int64Value
symbols.doc:
Int64Value builds a Value of kind int64. int and int32 callers should widen
to int64 at the call site.

symbols.name: IntValue
symbols.doc:
IntValue builds a Value of kind int64 from a plain int. Provided for caller
ergonomy so the most common integer type does not need an explicit cast.

symbols.name: Kind
symbols.doc:
Kind discriminates the payload variant carried by a Value. Kind values are
stable across the public API; new variants are appended at the end so old
handlers default to KindAny rather than panic on an unknown discriminant.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc:
String returns the lowercase textual label associated with the Kind
receiver, suitable for diagnostic dumps and golden test fixtures.
"string", "time", "uint64", "group" — or "unknown" for future variants.

symbols.name: KindAny
symbols.doc:
KindAny tags a Value whose payload is an unconstrained interface; handlers
SHOULD render it via fmt.Sprintf or a "?" placeholder when the concrete
type is not in their format table. It is also the zero-value of Kind.

symbols.name: KindBool
symbols.doc: KindBool tags a Value carrying a boolean payload.

symbols.name: KindDuration
symbols.doc: KindDuration tags a Value carrying a time.Duration payload.

symbols.name: KindFloat64
symbols.doc: KindFloat64 tags a Value carrying a float64 payload.

symbols.name: KindGroup
symbols.doc:
KindGroup tags a Value whose payload is a slice of AttrValue, used to model
nested groups (slog.Group) without flattening into the parent record.

symbols.name: KindInt64
symbols.doc: KindInt64 tags a Value carrying an int64 payload (also covers int / int32).

symbols.name: KindString
symbols.doc: KindString tags a Value carrying a string payload.

symbols.name: KindTime
symbols.doc: KindTime tags a Value carrying a time.Time payload.

symbols.name: KindUint64
symbols.doc: KindUint64 tags a Value carrying an unsigned 64-bit integer payload.

symbols.name: Logger
symbols.spelled: interface{Enabled(ctx context.Context, lv level.Level) (enabled bool); Log(ctx context.Context, lv level.Level, msg string, attrs ...AttrValue); With(attrs ...AttrValue) (child Logger); WithGroup(name string) (child Logger)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Enabled(ctx context.Context, lv github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger/level.Level) (enabled bool); Log(ctx context.Context, lv github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger/level.Level, msg string, attrs ...github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.AttrValue); With(attrs ...github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.AttrValue) (child github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.Logger); WithGroup(name string) (child github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.Logger)}
symbols.doc:
Logger is the primary logging interface. Implementations MUST be safe for
concurrent use by multiple goroutines.

symbols.name: Enabled
symbols.doc: Enabled reports whether a record at the given level would be emitted.

symbols.name: Log
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, lv level.Level, msg string, attrs ...AttrValue)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, lv github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger/level.Level, msg string, attrs ...github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.AttrValue)
symbols.doc:
Log emits a RecordEvent at the given level with the supplied message
and attrs. Implementations SHOULD short-circuit when Enabled returns
false to avoid unnecessary formatting work.

symbols.name: With
symbols.doc:
With returns a derived Logger whose emitted records always include the
supplied attrs. The receiver MUST NOT be mutated.

symbols.name: WithGroup
symbols.doc:
WithGroup returns a derived Logger whose subsequent attributes are
namespaced under the given group name. Empty names MUST be a no-op.

symbols.name: NewValue
symbols.doc:
NewValue is a generic alias of AnyValue, exposed for tooling that expects a
New-prefixed constructor on every exported type. Prefer the typed
constructors (StringValue, Int64Value, …) at call sites.

symbols.name: RecordEvent
symbols.spelled: struct{Time time.Time; Level level.Level; Message string; PC uintptr; Attrs []AttrValue; TraceContext TraceContextValue}
symbols.canonical: struct{Time time.Time; Level github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger/level.Level; Message string; PC uintptr; Attrs []github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.AttrValue; TraceContext github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.TraceContextValue}

fields.name: Time
fields.doc: Time is the instant the event occurred; zero means "fill in at handle time".

fields.name: Level
fields.doc: Level is the severity of the event.

fields.name: Message
fields.doc: Message is the human-readable description of the event.

fields.name: PC
Attrs
fields.doc: Attrs carries the structured key/value pairs attached to this event.

fields.name: TraceContext
fields.doc:
TraceContext is the identity of the span this event was emitted
inside; the zero value means "no trace here" and MUST render nothing.
It is a FIELD rather than two entries in Attrs because the Encoder
port receives no context.Context — the identity has to travel on the
record to reach the formatter at all — and because OpenTelemetry
prescribes trace_id / span_id as TOP-LEVEL keys of the log object,
which an attribute cannot be: WithGroup would prefix it. See ADR 0062.

symbols.doc:
RecordEvent captures a single log event; handlers are responsible for writing
or forwarding it. Instances are intended to be used read-only after
construction by the Logger implementation.

symbols.name: Sink
symbols.spelled: interface{Close() (err error); Flush(ctx context.Context) (err error); Write(ctx context.Context, r RecordEvent, p []byte) (n int, err error)}
symbols.canonical: interface{Close() (err error); Flush(ctx context.Context) (err error); Write(ctx context.Context, r github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.RecordEvent, p []byte) (n int, err error)}
symbols.doc:
Sink is the transport port consumed by the generic Handler. Implementations
MUST be safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines and SHOULD assume
their own concurrency model (mutex / lock-free / batched flush) so the
Handler can stay encoder-agnostic. Sinks that need the severity level read
it directly from r.Level — the port is intentionally kept narrow.

symbols.name: Close
symbols.doc:
Close releases any resources held by the sink (file descriptors, AWS
clients, network connections). Sinks MAY refuse subsequent Writes
after Close returns; callers MUST NOT use the sink after closing it.

symbols.name: Flush
symbols.doc: Flush forces any buffered records out. A no-op for synchronous sinks.

symbols.name: Write
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, r RecordEvent, p []byte) (n int, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, r github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/core/observe/logger.RecordEvent, p []byte) (n int, err error)
symbols.doc:
Write delivers the formatted byte payload p plus the originating record
to the underlying transport. Sinks MAY ignore p and re-serialise from
r when their wire protocol differs from the encoder's output (e.g. a
CloudWatch sink reads r.Time directly to populate the AWS request).

symbols.name: SinkRequired

code.public: Logger handler requires a non-nil sink

symbols.doc: SinkRequired is returned when NewHandler receives a nil Sink.

symbols.name: SpanIDHexLen
symbols.doc: SpanIDHexLen is the span identifier's length in lowercase hex.

symbols.name: SpanIDKey
symbols.doc: SpanIDKey is the top-level field name carrying the span identifier.

symbols.name: SpanIDLen
symbols.doc: SpanIDLen is the span identifier's length in bytes.

symbols.name: StringValue
symbols.doc: StringValue builds a Value of kind string.

symbols.name: TimeValue
symbols.doc:
TimeValue builds a Value of kind time. The time.Time payload lives in the
any field because its locale + monotonic representation does not fit into
num without additional storage.

symbols.name: TraceContextSource
symbols.doc:
TraceContextSource reads the trace context carried by ctx.

It is a FUNC port, so ADR 0039 is satisfied structurally: a func type cannot
grow a method, so publishing it can never break a downstream implementation.
It returns the zero (invalid) value rather than an error or an ok flag —
running outside a trace is the normal state of most code, not a fault, and
IsValid is the single question every caller already has to ask.

Implementations MUST NOT allocate: they run once per emitted record.

symbols.name: TraceContextValue

fields.name: TraceID
fields.doc: TraceID identifies the whole trace; rendered as 32 lowercase hex digits.

fields.name: SpanID
fields.doc: SpanID identifies the span within the trace; 16 lowercase hex digits.

symbols.doc:
TraceContextValue is the trace correlation a single log record carries: the
identity of the span the record was emitted inside.

It is a VALUE and carries no flags and no tracestate, because a log line
answers exactly one question — "which span produced this?" — and the
sampling decision that governs the trace is not a property of the line.

The zero value is the INVALID context, deliberately: an all-zero trace-id is
what W3C Trace Context §3.2.2.3 declares invalid, and an all-zero span-id is
§3.2.2.4's. So "no trace here" and "a trace nobody may join" are one value
with one spelling, and every consumer has exactly one check to make.

symbols.name: AppendSpanIDHex
symbols.doc:
AppendSpanIDHex appends the span identifier to dst as 16 lowercase hex
digits and returns the extended buffer. Same contract as AppendTraceIDHex.

symbols.name: AppendTraceIDHex
symbols.doc:
AppendTraceIDHex appends the trace identifier to dst as 32 LOWERCASE hex
digits and returns the extended buffer.

The spelling is normative — "Trace IDs and span IDs must be lowercase and
hex-encoded" (specification/compatibility/logging_trace_context.md) — and
three formatters (the text encoder, the JSON encoder and the legacy text
handler) have to agree on it byte for byte, which is why it lives beside the
value rather than three times over in internal/service/observe/logger.

It appends and never returns a string: a string would be one heap allocation
per emitted record, and the logger's one-allocation-per-emit contract has no
room for a second. See ADR 0062 and pkg/v1/observe/logger/BENCH.md.

symbols.name: IsValid
symbols.doc:
IsValid reports whether the pair names a span a backend can join: both
identifiers present and non-zero.

Both are required rather than either, and that follows the data model rather
than convenience: "if a SpanId is provided, the corresponding TraceId should
also be included" (specification/logs/data-model.md, Trace Context Fields).
The only producer in this SDK is a W3C span context, which is itself invalid
unless both identifiers are set, so a half-populated pair never reaches an
encoder through a supported path — and if one is forged by hand, emitting
half of it would produce a field no query can join on.

symbols.name: TraceIDHexLen
symbols.doc: TraceIDHexLen is the trace identifier's length in lowercase hex.

symbols.name: TraceIDKey
symbols.doc: TraceIDKey is the top-level field name carrying the trace identifier.

symbols.name: TraceIDLen
symbols.doc: TraceIDLen is the trace identifier's length in bytes.

symbols.name: Uint64Value
symbols.doc: Uint64Value builds a Value of kind uint64.

symbols.name: Value
symbols.doc:
Value is an immutable discriminated payload attached to an AttrValue. Use
the documented constructors (StringValue / Int64Value / …) to obtain a
well-formed instance — the zero value is a valid KindAny carrying nil.

symbols.name: Any
symbols.doc:
Any returns the opaque payload for KindAny. For typed Kinds the return is
nil — callers should call the typed accessor instead.

symbols.name: Bits
symbols.doc:
Bits returns the raw uint64 storage that backs all bit-packed Kinds
(KindBool / KindInt64 / KindUint64 / KindFloat64 / KindDuration). Callers
SHOULD prefer the typed accessors; Bits exists for tooling and tests that
need direct access to the packed storage.

symbols.name: Bool
symbols.doc:
Bool returns the boolean payload. The result is undefined when Kind is not
KindBool; callers MUST guard with Kind() before calling this accessor.

symbols.name: Duration
symbols.doc:
Duration returns the time.Duration payload. The result is undefined when
Kind is not KindDuration; callers MUST guard with Kind() before calling
this accessor.

symbols.name: Float64
symbols.doc:
Float64 returns the float64 payload. The result is undefined when Kind is
not KindFloat64; callers MUST guard with Kind() before calling this
accessor.

symbols.name: Group
symbols.doc:
Group returns the nested AttrValue slice. The result is undefined when
Kind is not KindGroup; callers MUST guard with Kind() before calling this
accessor. A nil any field decodes as a nil slice.

symbols.name: Int64
symbols.doc:
Int64 returns the int64 payload. The result is undefined when Kind is not
KindInt64; callers MUST guard with Kind() before calling this accessor.

symbols.name: Kind
symbols.doc:
Kind returns the discriminator for this Value, indicating which typed
accessor (String / Int64 / Float64 / …) handlers should call.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc:
String returns the textual payload when the Value carries KindString; for
any other Kind it returns an empty string. Handlers that need a stringified
rendering of non-string Kinds MUST format from the typed accessor instead.

symbols.name: Time
symbols.doc:
Time returns the time.Time payload. The result is undefined when Kind is
not KindTime; callers MUST guard with Kind() before calling this accessor.
A nil any field decodes as the zero time.Time.

symbols.name: Uint64
symbols.doc:
Uint64 returns the uint64 payload. The result is undefined when Kind is not
KindUint64; callers MUST guard with Kind() before calling this accessor.

symbols.name: WriteFailed

code.public: Log write failed

symbols.doc: WriteFailed wraps the underlying writer's error at Handle time.

symbols.name: WriterNil

code.public: Log handler requires a non-nil writer

symbols.doc: WriterNil is returned when NewTextHandler receives a nil io.Writer.

symbols.name: CodeLevelUnknown
symbols.doc:
CodeLevelUnknown identifies a ParseLevel call whose input does not match any
of the four canonical lowercase level names (debug / info / warn / error).

symbols.name: Debug
symbols.doc: Debug represents detailed tracing information useful during development.

symbols.name: Error
symbols.doc: Error represents failures that usually signal a broken invariant and require action.

symbols.name: Info
symbols.doc: Info represents routine operational events occurring during normal execution.

symbols.name: Level
symbols.doc: Level represents the importance of a log record; higher values are more severe.

symbols.name: String
symbols.doc: String returns the uppercase textual label associated with the Level receiver.

symbols.name: LevelUnknown

code.public: log level name is not recognised

symbols.doc:
LevelUnknown is returned by ParseLevel when the input string does not name
one of the four canonical levels (debug / info / warn / error). The offending
input is intentionally not echoed into the error so a hostile config value
cannot leak through the message; callers parsing untrusted env/config strings
get a stable, redaction-safe sentinel matchable via errs.HasCode or errors.Is.

symbols.name: Leveler
symbols.doc:
Leveler exposes a single live severity threshold. A gate or sink consults
Level on each record so the floor can change at runtime, instead of freezing
a value at construction. Var is the canonical atomic implementation; any
constant threshold can satisfy the interface by returning a fixed Level.

symbols.name: Level
symbols.doc:
Level reports the current threshold; implementations MUST be safe for
concurrent callers reading while another goroutine mutates the value.

symbols.name: NewVar
symbols.doc:
NewVar returns a Var initialised to initial. The returned pointer is the
Leveler a gate or sink holds; callers later retune it with Set.

symbols.name: ParseLevel
symbols.doc:
ParseLevel maps a canonical lowercase level name to its Level constant. It is
the inverse of Level.String lowercased: "debug", "info", "warn", and "error"
round-trip to Debug, Info, Warn, and Error respectively. Input is trimmed of
surrounding whitespace and lowercased before matching, so "INFO" and " Warn "
resolve too. Any other input yields the zero Level and the LevelUnknown
sentinel, so callers parse an env/config string then feed the result to Var.Set.

symbols.name: Var
symbols.doc:
Var is an atomically mutable Level holder satisfying Leveler. Its zero value
is ready to use and reports Info (the Level zero value), so a freshly
declared Var gates at the same default as a config's unset MinLevel. Set and
Level are safe for concurrent use; a gate may read Level on the hot path
while a control goroutine raises or lowers the floor via Set.

symbols.name: Level
symbols.doc:
Level reports the current threshold. The load is atomic and lock-free,
keeping it cheap enough for a per-record gate to call on the hot path.

symbols.name: Set
symbols.doc:
Set replaces the current threshold with lvl. The store is atomic, so a
concurrent Level caller observes either the old or the new value, never a
torn read.

symbols.name: Warn
symbols.doc: Warn represents abnormal but recoverable conditions worth human attention.

symbols.name: BufferFull

code.public: Async sink ring buffer is full

symbols.doc:
BufferFull is returned by Write under the DropNewest policy when the
ring is saturated; the entry is dropped and the OnDrop callback fires.

symbols.name: CodeAsyncBufferFull
symbols.doc:
CodeAsyncBufferFull identifies a Write call where the policy is DropNewest
and the ring is saturated; the entry is dropped and the OnDrop callback
fires for the caller's metric pipeline.

symbols.name: CodeAsyncCtxCancelled
symbols.doc:
CodeAsyncCtxCancelled identifies a Write or Flush call whose context was
already done. Wraps the stdlib context error so the typed-errors-only SDK
rule is satisfied and consumers can HasCode / errors.Is against it.

symbols.name: CodeAsyncStopped
symbols.doc:
CodeAsyncStopped identifies a Write call after Close has terminated the
drainer goroutine — the buffered queue can no longer accept work.

symbols.name: CtxCancelled

code.public: Async sink aborted due to cancellation

symbols.doc:
CtxCancelled wraps a context that was already done when Write or
Flush was entered. Provided as a typed sentinel so consumers match
via HasCode / errors.Is without reaching for stdlib context errors.

symbols.name: Stopped

code.public: Async sink is stopped

symbols.doc:
Stopped is returned by Write after Close has stopped the drainer
goroutine. Subsequent Write calls drop the payload immediately.

symbols.name: CodeEncWriteSealFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeEncWriteSealFailed identifies a record whose per-sink subkey could not be
derived or whose bytes could not be sealed before delivery to the downstream
sink.

symbols.name: CodeFramingFailed
symbols.doc:
CodeFramingFailed identifies a sealed box too large for the 4-byte big-endian
length prefix the byte framing prepends.

symbols.name: EncWriteSealFailed

code.public: Encrypting middleware could not seal the record

symbols.doc:
EncWriteSealFailed wraps a subkey-derivation or Seal failure raised while
encrypting a record's bytes before delivery to the downstream sink.

symbols.name: FramingFailed

code.public: Encrypting middleware could not frame the sealed record

symbols.name: CodeFailoverEmpty

CodeFailoverExhausted identifies a Write call where every downstream
sink in the failover chain returned a non-nil error. The sentinel wraps
errors.Join of the per-sink failures so callers can inspect each cause.

symbols.doc: Empty is returned when New is invoked without any downstream sinks.

Exhausted wraps an errors.Join of every per-sink failure when the
failover chain has tried every downstream Sink without success.

symbols.doc:
CodeFanoutWriteFailed identifies a Write call where one or more of the

against the individual sink sentinels.

symbols.doc:
FanoutWriteFailed wraps an errors.Join of the per-sink failures captured
during a fan-out Write. The wrapped cause exposes each individual sink's
error chain through errors.Unwrap, so consumers can inspect every fanout
branch via errors.Is.

Write / Flush / Close. The error's Fields carries panic_type (the
recovered value's dynamic type name); the rendered panic value lives in
the error's log-only Private field, never in Fields.

symbols.name: CodeRouteNoMatch

symbols.name: NoMatch

symbols.doc:
NoMatch is returned by Write when no predicate matched the record AND
no default sink was configured. Callers that want a catch-all should
pass a default sink to New so writes never silently disappear.
